glossary.definition: Element that is lustrous, malleable, ductile, and generally good conductor of heat and electricity.
Element that is generally dull, brittle, and poor conductor (with exceptions like graphite).
Property of metals to be beaten into thin sheets.
Property of metals to be drawn into thin wires.
Arrangement of metals in order of decreasing reactivity.
Compound formed by transfer of electrons between metal and non-metal ions.
Mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably.
Gradual destruction of metals by reaction with environment (e.g. rusting of iron).
Coating iron/steel with zinc to prevent rusting.

concepts.name: What are metals?
concepts.simple_answer: Metals are elements that are generally lustrous, malleable, ductile, and good conductors of heat and electricity.
concepts.why: Foundation of Ch 3 — metals introduced first.
concepts.example: Iron, copper, aluminium, gold, and silver are familiar metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Not every metal shows all properties — mercury is liquid at room temperature.

concepts.name: What are non-metals?
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals are elements that are generally dull, brittle, and poor conductors — with exceptions like graphite and iodine.
concepts.example: Carbon, sulphur, oxygen, and chlorine are non-metals.
concepts.remember: Dull + brittle + poor conductor = non-metal clues.
concepts.common_confusion: Graphite conducts electricity — important exception.

concepts.name: Elements classified as metals or non-metals
concepts.simple_answer: About 80% of known elements are metals; rest are non-metals or metalloids on the zig-zag line of the periodic table.
concepts.example: Left and centre of periodic table = mostly metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Metalloids (Si, Ge) show properties of both.

concepts.name: Physical vs chemical properties
concepts.simple_answer: Physical properties (lustre, hardness) can be observed without changing substance; chemical properties (reactivity) need a reaction.
concepts.example: Shining copper is physical; copper turning green is chemical.
concepts.remember: Physical = no new substance; chemical = reaction.
concepts.common_confusion: Both types matter in Ch 3 exams.

concepts.name: Activity 3.1 preview — appearance and hardness
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.1: collect samples of metals and non-metals; observe lustre, hardness, and surface.
concepts.example: Compare iron nail, copper wire, sulphur lump, and carbon.
concepts.remember: Observe before you react — physical properties first.
concepts.common_confusion: Handle samples safely — some are powders or brittle.

concepts.name: Common metal samples in Ch 3
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT uses iron, copper, aluminium, magnesium, zinc, lead, and sodium/potassium for reactions.
concepts.why: Know the substances used in activities.
concepts.example: Magnesium ribbon burns with dazzling white flame.
concepts.remember: Memorise the common metal list for equations.
concepts.common_confusion: Sodium and potassium stored under kerosene — very reactive.

concepts.name: Common non-metal samples in Ch 3
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT uses sulphur, carbon (graphite/diamond), iodine, oxygen, and chlorine in examples.
concepts.example: Sulphur is yellow solid; iodine is grey-black solid.
concepts.remember: S, C, I, O, Cl appear throughout chapter.
concepts.common_confusion: Iodine sublimes — solid to vapour directly.

concepts.name: Uses of metals in daily life
concepts.simple_answer: Metals used in utensils, wires, construction, jewellery, and vehicles because of strength and conductivity.
concepts.example: Copper wires carry electricity; aluminium foils wrap food.
concepts.common_confusion: Alloys (steel, brass) often used instead of pure metals.

concepts.name: Uses of non-metals in daily life
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals essential for life — oxygen for breathing, nitrogen in fertilisers, carbon in all living matter.
concepts.example: Graphite in pencil lead; sulphur in matches.
concepts.remember: Non-metals in air, food, and industry.
concepts.common_confusion: Chlorine disinfects drinking water.

concepts.name: Chapter 3 roadmap
concepts.simple_answer: Ch 3 covers physical properties, reactions with air/water/acids, reactivity series, ionic bonding, extraction, and corrosion.
concepts.example: Activities 3.1–3.6 in lab sections.

days.title: Physical Properties of Metals — Lustre and Hardness

concepts.name: Metallic lustre
concepts.simple_answer: Metals have a shining surface called metallic lustre when freshly cut or polished.
concepts.example: Freshly cut copper looks reddish-brown and shiny.
concepts.common_confusion: Tarnished metals lose lustre due to surface oxide layer.

concepts.name: Why metals appear lustrous
concepts.simple_answer: Metals reflect light strongly from their surface because of free electrons in the metal lattice.
concepts.example: Gold jewellery shines because of metallic bonding.
concepts.common_confusion: Non-metals generally do not reflect light this way.

concepts.name: Activity 3.1 — testing lustre
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.1: observe iron, copper, aluminium, magnesium, and zinc for lustre; compare with sulphur and carbon.
concepts.example: Iron nail shiny when new; sulphur dull yellow.
concepts.common_confusion: Clean surface with sandpaper before observing lustre.

concepts.name: Hardness of metals
concepts.simple_answer: Most metals are hard — cannot be cut with a knife; exceptions: sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut.
concepts.example: Iron and copper are hard; sodium cuts with knife.
concepts.remember: Hardness varies — alkali metals are soft.
concepts.common_confusion: Hardness is not the same as strength.

concepts.name: Hardness of non-metals
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals are generally soft (sulphur, iodine) or very hard (diamond — allotrope of carbon).
concepts.example: Diamond is hardest natural substance — carbon non-metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Diamond hardness is exception — most non-metals brittle.

concepts.name: Activity 3.1 — hardness comparison
concepts.simple_answer: Try cutting samples with knife — sodium/potassium cut easily; iron, copper, and zinc do not.
concepts.example: Only alkali metals among samples cut with knife.
concepts.common_confusion: Never cut sodium without teacher supervision — reacts with moisture.

concepts.name: State of metals at room temperature
concepts.simple_answer: Most metals are solid at room temperature; mercury (Hg) is the only liquid metal.
concepts.example: Mercury used in thermometers (being phased out).
concepts.remember: Hg is liquid metal — unique exception.
concepts.common_confusion: Gallium melts in hand — slightly above room temp.

concepts.name: State of non-metals at room temperature
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals exist as solids (S, C, I), liquids (bromine), or gases (O₂, N₂, Cl₂) at room temperature.
concepts.example: Bromine is red-brown liquid non-metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Bromine fumes are toxic — avoid inhalation.

concepts.name: Compare lustre — metal vs non-metal
concepts.simple_answer: Metals: lustrous (shiny). Non-metals: generally non-lustrous (dull) — iodine has slight lustre.
concepts.example: Compare polished copper with sulphur lump.
concepts.remember: Lustre is quick visual test for classification.
concepts.common_confusion: Iodine crystals show metallic lustre — rare for non-metals.

concepts.name: Exam — lustre and hardness
concepts.simple_answer: Define lustre → give metal example → define hardness → compare Na (soft) with Fe (hard) → Activity 3.1 observations.
concepts.example: Fresh iron shiny; sulphur dull and soft.
concepts.common_confusion: Always mention mercury as liquid metal if asked about state.

concepts.name: Malleability definition
concepts.simple_answer: Malleability is the property of metals to be beaten into thin sheets without breaking.
concepts.example: Gold beaten into gold leaf for decoration.
concepts.common_confusion: Non-metals are not malleable — they crumble.

concepts.name: Activity 3.2 — malleability test
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.2: beat iron, copper, aluminium, and zinc with hammer — form thin sheets.
concepts.example: Aluminium foil is malleable aluminium sheet.
concepts.remember: Metals form sheets; non-metals powder or break.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not hammer sodium — dangerous reaction with moisture.

concepts.name: Gold and silver malleability
concepts.simple_answer: Gold is most malleable — beaten into extremely thin sheets; silver also highly malleable.
concepts.example: Gold leaf on temple domes and picture frames.
concepts.remember: Au and Ag most malleable metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Malleability explains use in jewellery and leaf.

concepts.name: Ductility definition
concepts.simple_answer: Ductility is the property of metals to be drawn into thin wires without breaking.
concepts.example: Copper and aluminium wires in electrical cables.
concepts.common_confusion: Non-metals cannot be drawn into wires.

concepts.name: Activity 3.2 — ductility test
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.2: try drawing copper and aluminium into wires — metals extend without snapping.
concepts.example: Copper wire in motor winding.
concepts.remember: Metals form wires; sulphur breaks if pulled.
concepts.common_confusion: Gold wire used in micro-electronics — very ductile.

concepts.name: Copper and aluminium wires
concepts.simple_answer: Copper is excellent electrical conductor — used in household wiring; aluminium in overhead power lines.

visual.label: Cu and Al wires — daily use

concepts.example: Overhead cables on streets are aluminium.
concepts.common_confusion: Al lighter than Cu — preferred for long spans.

concepts.name: Sonority definition
concepts.simple_answer: Sonority is the property of metals to produce a ringing sound when struck hard.
concepts.example: School bell and temple bell are metal — sonorous.
concepts.common_confusion: Non-metals do not ring — dull thud.

concepts.name: Activity 3.2 — sonority test
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.2: strike iron, copper, and aluminium — hear ringing; strike sulphur or carbon — dull sound.
concepts.example: Bell metal (bronze alloy) rings clearly.
concepts.common_confusion: Sonority explains use of metals in bells and gongs.

concepts.name: Malleability vs ductility
concepts.simple_answer: Malleability = beaten into sheets (hammer). Ductility = drawn into wires (pulling). Both show metal plasticity.
concepts.example: Al foil = malleable; copper wire = ductile.
concepts.common_confusion: Gold is both most malleable and very ductile.

concepts.name: Exam — malleability, ductility, sonority
concepts.simple_answer: Define all three → Activity 3.2 for each → examples: gold leaf (malleable), copper wire (ductile), bell (sonorous).
concepts.example: Non-metals fail all three tests — contrast.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse malleability with ductility.

days.title: Heat and Electrical Conductivity of Metals

concepts.name: Heat conductivity of metals
concepts.simple_answer: Metals are good conductors of heat — heat passes quickly through metal.
concepts.example: Metal spoon in hot tea gets hot quickly.
concepts.common_confusion: Used in cooking pans and radiators.

concepts.name: Activity 3.3 — heat conductivity
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.3: hold metal rod in flame — heat reaches far end quickly; compare with non-metal rod.
concepts.example: Iron rod end gets hot when one end is heated.
concepts.remember: Metal rod conducts heat along length.
concepts.common_confusion: Use tongs — metal gets very hot.

concepts.name: Electrical conductivity of metals
concepts.simple_answer: Metals are good conductors of electricity — allow electric current to pass through easily.
concepts.example: Copper wires in household electrical circuits.
concepts.remember: Free electrons carry current in metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Basis for all electrical wiring.

concepts.name: Activity 3.3 — electrical conductivity
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.3: connect iron, copper, and aluminium in circuit with bulb — bulb glows; try sulphur or carbon — no glow.
concepts.example: Bulb glows with metal in circuit.
concepts.remember: Metals complete circuit; most non-metals do not.
concepts.common_confusion: Use low voltage battery for safety.

concepts.name: Why metals conduct electricity
concepts.simple_answer: Metal atoms have loosely held valence electrons (free electrons) that move and carry electric charge.
concepts.example: Same free electrons explain heat conduction.
concepts.common_confusion: Insulators lack free electrons.

concepts.name: Uses of heat conductivity
concepts.simple_answer: Metal cooking pans, radiators, and heat sinks use high thermal conductivity.
concepts.example: Copper bottom pans heat food evenly.
concepts.common_confusion: Handles often plastic or wood — insulators.

concepts.name: Uses of electrical conductivity
concepts.simple_answer: Copper and aluminium wires, electrical contacts, and circuit boards use metal conductors.
concepts.example: Every electrical appliance has metal wires.
concepts.remember: Conductors carry current in all circuits.
concepts.common_confusion: Gold plating on connectors — resists corrosion.

concepts.name: Compare conductivity — metals vs non-metals
concepts.simple_answer: Metals: good conductors of heat and electricity. Non-metals: generally poor conductors (insulators).

visual.formula: Metal: good conductor | Non-metal: poor conductor

concepts.example: Iron conducts; sulphur does not.
concepts.common_confusion: Graphite and iodine are exceptions — see Day 5.

concepts.name: Activity 3.3 summary
concepts.simple_answer: Activity 3.3 confirms metals conduct heat and electricity; non-metals (except graphite) do not.
concepts.example: Three tests: heat rod, electric circuit, compare.
concepts.remember: Both heat and electrical tests on same metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Graphite exception tested separately in Activity 3.4.

concepts.name: Exam — conductivity of metals
concepts.simple_answer: State metals are good conductors → explain free electrons → Activity 3.3 → uses (wires, pans) → contrast non-metals.
concepts.example: Cu wires + metal pan as two examples.
concepts.remember: Free electrons link heat and electrical conduction.
concepts.common_confusion: Mention graphite exception briefly.

concepts.name: Physical properties of non-metals — overview
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals are generally dull, brittle, non-sonorous, and poor conductors of heat and electricity.
concepts.example: Sulphur is dull, brittle, and insulator.
concepts.common_confusion: Exceptions exist — always note graphite and iodine.

concepts.name: Non-metals are dull (non-lustrous)
concepts.simple_answer: Most non-metals have dull surfaces without metallic shine — sulphur is yellow but not lustrous.
concepts.example: Compare shiny copper with dull sulphur lump.
concepts.remember: No metallic lustre on most non-metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Iodine crystals show slight lustre — exception.

concepts.name: Non-metals are brittle
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals break into pieces when hammered — not malleable or ductile.
concepts.example: Sulphur crumbles when hammered.
concepts.common_confusion: Diamond is hard but still brittle — shatters.

concepts.name: Activity 3.4 — non-metal properties
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.4: test sulphur and carbon — dull, brittle, non-sonorous, do not conduct (except graphite).
concepts.example: Sulphur powder after hammering.
concepts.remember: All four properties tested on non-metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Graphite tested separately for conductivity.

concepts.name: Non-metals poor heat conductors
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals are bad conductors of heat — insulators; wood and plastic handles stay cool.
concepts.example: Wooden spoon stays cool in hot soup.
concepts.remember: Heat does not pass easily through non-metals.
concepts.common_confusion: Air (mixture) is also poor conductor — wool traps air.

concepts.name: Non-metals poor electrical conductors
concepts.simple_answer: Most non-metals do not conduct electricity — used as insulators in cables and equipment.
concepts.example: Rubber and plastic coating on wires.
concepts.remember: No free electrons → no current flow.
concepts.common_confusion: Insulators protect from electric shock.

concepts.name: Exception — graphite conducts electricity
concepts.simple_answer: Graphite (allotrope of carbon) conducts electricity — used in pencil lead and electrodes.
concepts.example: Dry cell electrode contains graphite.
concepts.common_confusion: Graphite conducts but sulphur and diamond do not.

concepts.name: Exception — iodine lustre
concepts.simple_answer: Iodine is a non-metal with lustrous grey-black crystals — sublimes on heating.
concepts.example: Iodine tincture used as antiseptic.
concepts.remember: Iodine has metallic appearance but is non-metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Iodine sublimes — solid to vapour without melting.

concepts.name: Allotropes of carbon
concepts.simple_answer: Carbon exists as diamond (hard, insulator) and graphite (soft, conductor) — same element, different properties.

visual.formula: Diamond: hard, insulator | Graphite: soft, conductor

concepts.example: Pencil lead is graphite; diamond in jewellery.
concepts.common_confusion: Fullerene and graphene beyond Class 10 scope.

concepts.name: Exam — non-metal physical properties
concepts.simple_answer: List dull, brittle, non-sonorous, poor conductor → Activity 3.4 → exceptions: graphite (conducts), iodine (lustrous).
concepts.example: Always mention graphite and iodine exceptions.
concepts.remember: Four properties + two exceptions = full marks.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not say all non-metals are gases — many are solids.

days.title: Metals Burned in Air — Metal Oxides

concepts.name: Metals react with oxygen in air
concepts.simple_answer: Most metals combine with oxygen when heated or burned to form metal oxides.
concepts.example: Magnesium burns with dazzling white flame.
concepts.common_confusion: Some oxides protective; others flaky.

concepts.name: Activity 3.5 — burning magnesium
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.5: burn magnesium ribbon in air — dazzling white flame; white ash MgO forms.
concepts.example: Mg ribbon cleaned with sandpaper before burning.
concepts.common_confusion: Never look directly at burning Mg — very bright.

concepts.name: Activity 3.5 — burning copper
concepts.simple_answer: Heat copper wire in flame — black copper(II) oxide CuO forms on surface.
concepts.example: Copper vessel bottom turns black on heating.
concepts.common_confusion: Green patina on old copper is basic carbonate — not Day 6 focus.

concepts.name: Activity 3.5 — burning aluminium
concepts.simple_answer: Aluminium forms white aluminium oxide Al₂O₃ layer — protects metal from further corrosion.
concepts.example: Aluminium utensils resist rust due to Al₂O₃ layer.
concepts.common_confusion: Anodised aluminium has thicker oxide layer.

concepts.name: Iron burns in air
concepts.simple_answer: Iron does not burn easily in air at room temperature but forms rust slowly; iron filings burn in flame.
concepts.example: Iron filings spark in Bunsen flame.
concepts.remember: Iron rusts slowly at room temperature.
concepts.common_confusion: Rust is hydrated iron oxide — Day 15 detail.

concepts.name: Sodium and potassium in air
concepts.simple_answer: Sodium and potassium react vigorously with oxygen at room temperature — stored under kerosene.
concepts.example: Na cut surface tarnishes instantly in air.
concepts.remember: Never leave Na/K exposed to air.
concepts.common_confusion: K reacts even faster than Na with oxygen.

concepts.name: Metal oxides are generally basic
concepts.simple_answer: Metal oxides are basic in nature — turn red litmus blue; react with acids (links Ch 2).
concepts.example: MgO reacts with HCl — neutralisation type.
concepts.common_confusion: Amphoteric oxides (Al₂O₃, ZnO) are exceptions.

concepts.name: Non-metals burn in air
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metals combine with oxygen to form non-metal oxides — often acidic or neutral.
concepts.example: S + O₂ → SO₂; C + O₂ → CO₂.
concepts.common_confusion: SO₂ and CO₂ dissolve in water forming acids.

concepts.name: Compare metal vs non-metal oxides
concepts.simple_answer: Metal oxides: basic (MgO, CuO). Non-metal oxides: acidic (CO₂, SO₂).

visual.formula: Metal oxide: basic | Non-metal oxide: acidic

concepts.example: MgO basic; CO₂ forms carbonic acid in water.
concepts.remember: Basic vs acidic oxides — opposite nature.
concepts.common_confusion: CO and N₂O are neutral oxides — exceptions.

concepts.name: Exam — metals burned in air
concepts.simple_answer: General equation → Mg, Cu, Al examples with balanced equations → Activity 3.5 → basic nature of metal oxides.
concepts.example: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO with white flame observation.
concepts.common_confusion: Balance all equations for full marks.

concepts.name: Metals react with water — overview
concepts.simple_answer: Some metals react with water to form metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas; reactivity varies greatly.
concepts.example: Sodium reacts violently with cold water.
concepts.remember: Not all metals react with water.
concepts.common_confusion: Product depends on metal reactivity.

concepts.name: Sodium with cold water
concepts.simple_answer: Sodium reacts vigorously with cold water — moves on surface, melts, H₂ gas evolved, solution alkaline.
concepts.example: Na piece fizzes and may catch fire.
concepts.common_confusion: Never add large Na piece to water unsupervised.

concepts.name: Potassium with cold water
concepts.simple_answer: Potassium reacts even more vigorously than sodium — catches fire with lilac flame.
concepts.example: K explodes on water surface.
concepts.remember: K faster than Na — lower in series but same group.
concepts.common_confusion: Lilac flame colour characteristic of potassium.

concepts.name: Calcium with cold water
concepts.simple_answer: Calcium reacts with cold water moderately — bubbles of H₂, milky Ca(OH)₂ solution.
concepts.example: Ca(OH)₂ is limewater — turns milky with CO₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Milky suspension — Ca(OH)₂ slightly soluble.

concepts.name: Magnesium with hot water
concepts.simple_answer: Magnesium reacts slowly with hot water or steam — Mg(OH)₂ and H₂ formed.
concepts.example: Mg ribbon in boiling water reacts slowly.
concepts.remember: Mg needs hot water — not cold.
concepts.common_confusion: Mg(OH)₂ is milk of magnesia — antacid.

concepts.name: Iron with steam
concepts.simple_answer: Iron reacts with steam at high temperature to form iron(II,III) oxide and hydrogen.
concepts.example: Iron glows red hot in steam — H₂ collected.
concepts.remember: Fe does not react with cold water.
concepts.common_confusion: Fe₃O₄ is magnetic iron oxide.

concepts.name: Less reactive metals and water
concepts.simple_answer: Aluminium, zinc, and lead do not react with cold or hot water; aluminium reacts with steam.
concepts.example: Al foil does not react with water at room temp.
concepts.common_confusion: Copper, silver, gold — no reaction with water.

concepts.name: Testing hydrogen from metal + water
concepts.simple_answer: Bring burning splint to gas — hydrogen burns with pop sound.
concepts.why: Same test as Ch 2 acid + metal.
concepts.example: Pop sound confirms H₂ from Na + water.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not confuse with oxygen — relights splint.

concepts.name: Activity 3.6 — metals and water
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.6: add Na, Ca, Mg, Fe, Cu to water — observe which react and how vigorously.
concepts.example: Only Na, K, Ca react with cold water visibly.
concepts.remember: Compare vigour: K > Na > Ca > Mg (hot) > Fe (steam).
concepts.common_confusion: Cu placed in water — no reaction.

concepts.name: Exam — metals and water
concepts.simple_answer: General equation → Na, Ca, Mg, Fe examples with conditions (cold/hot/steam) → H₂ pop test → reactivity trend.
concepts.example: State water temperature needed for each metal.
concepts.remember: Conditions matter — cold vs hot vs steam.
concepts.common_confusion: Cu, Ag, Au — no reaction with water.

concepts.name: Metal + acid — general reaction
concepts.simple_answer: Acid reacts with reactive metal to give salt and hydrogen gas.
concepts.example: Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Only metals above H in reactivity series.

concepts.name: Zinc and dilute HCl
concepts.simple_answer: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ — bubbles of hydrogen, zinc dissolves.
concepts.example: Activity in Ch 2 and Ch 3 context.
concepts.common_confusion: Copper below hydrogen — no reaction with dilute HCl.

concepts.name: Iron and dilute H₂SO₄
concepts.simple_answer: Fe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂ — iron nails produce hydrogen slowly.
concepts.example: Pale green FeSO₄ solution forms.
concepts.common_confusion: Conc. HNO₃ may not give H₂ — oxidising acid.

concepts.name: Magnesium and dilute acid
concepts.simple_answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ — vigorous reaction, hydrogen evolved rapidly.
concepts.why: More reactive than Zn and Fe.
concepts.example: Mg ribbon reacts faster than Zn.
concepts.common_confusion: Reaction exothermic — test tube warms.

concepts.name: Aluminium and dilute acid
concepts.simple_answer: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂ — aluminium reacts after oxide layer removed.
concepts.example: Sandpaper Al before acid test.
concepts.common_confusion: AlCl₃ dissolved in water — aluminium chloride.

concepts.name: Copper and dilute acid — no reaction
concepts.simple_answer: Copper does not react with dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ — below hydrogen in reactivity series.
concepts.example: Cu metal placed in HCl — no bubbles.
concepts.remember: Cu cannot displace H from dilute acid.
concepts.common_confusion: Hot conc. HNO₃ reacts with Cu — different reaction.

concepts.name: Testing hydrogen gas
concepts.simple_answer: Bring burning splint to mouth of tube — hydrogen burns with characteristic pop sound.
concepts.example: Pop sound = H₂ confirmed.
concepts.remember: Same test for acid + metal and water + metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Oxygen relights glowing splint — different test.

concepts.name: Salt name from acid
concepts.simple_answer: HCl → chloride; H₂SO₄ → sulphate; HNO₃ → nitrate — acid determines salt anion.
concepts.example: Zn + HCl → zinc chloride.
concepts.remember: Anion from acid names the salt.
concepts.common_confusion: Same naming as Ch 2.

concepts.name: Reactivity and acid reaction
concepts.simple_answer: More reactive metals react faster and more vigorously with dilute acids.
concepts.example: Mg reacts faster than Zn; Zn faster than Fe.
concepts.common_confusion: Ag and Au do not react with dilute acids.

concepts.name: Exam — metal + acid
concepts.simple_answer: General equation → Zn/Fe/Mg examples → H₂ pop test → explain why Cu does not react → reactivity series link.
concepts.example: Three-part: equation + salt name + H₂ test.
concepts.remember: Cu no reaction — below hydrogen — key point.
concepts.common_confusion: Balance equations for full marks.

days.title: Displacement Reactions and Metal Salt Solutions

concepts.name: Displacement reaction definition
concepts.simple_answer: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.

visual.formula: More reactive metal + Salt of less reactive metal → Displacement

concepts.example: Zinc displaces copper from CuSO₄ solution.
concepts.common_confusion: No reaction if metal is less reactive than salt metal.

concepts.name: Zinc and copper sulphate
concepts.simple_answer: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu — iron grey zinc displaces red-brown copper.
concepts.example: Blue CuSO₄ solution becomes colourless ZnSO₄.
concepts.remember: Zn more reactive than Cu — displacement occurs.
concepts.common_confusion: Copper deposits as red-brown solid on zinc.

concepts.name: Iron and copper sulphate
concepts.simple_answer: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu — iron displaces copper from blue solution.
concepts.example: Iron nail in CuSO₄ gets copper coating.
concepts.remember: Fe above Cu in reactivity series.
concepts.common_confusion: Pale green FeSO₄ solution forms.

concepts.name: Copper and zinc sulphate — no reaction
concepts.simple_answer: Copper cannot displace zinc from ZnSO₄ — Cu less reactive than Zn.
concepts.example: Cu metal in ZnSO₄ — no change.
concepts.remember: Less reactive cannot displace more reactive.
concepts.common_confusion: Predicting no reaction is exam skill.

concepts.name: Silver and copper sulphate — no reaction
concepts.simple_answer: Silver does not displace copper from CuSO₄ — Ag less reactive than Cu.
concepts.example: Ag coin in CuSO₄ — no reaction.
concepts.remember: Ag near bottom of reactivity series.
concepts.common_confusion: Gold also does not displace copper.

concepts.name: Observations in displacement
concepts.simple_answer: Colour change in solution, metal deposit on strip, original metal dissolves or reacts.
concepts.example: Blue → colourless + red-brown Cu on Zn.
concepts.remember: Watch solution colour and metal coating.
concepts.common_confusion: Write observations before equation in exam.

concepts.name: Activity 3.7 — displacement reactions
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Activity 3.7: place Zn, Fe, Cu, Ag in various salt solutions — observe displacement.
concepts.example: Test Zn in CuSO₄, Cu in ZnSO₄, Fe in CuSO₄.
concepts.remember: More reactive metal in less reactive salt.
concepts.common_confusion: Systematic table of metal vs salt results.

concepts.name: Displacement and reactivity series
concepts.simple_answer: Displacement reactions prove and use the reactivity series — higher displaces lower.

visual.formula: If Metal A > Metal B → A displaces B from B's salt

concepts.example: Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag order confirmed by displacement.
concepts.common_confusion: Single displacement — one metal swaps.

concepts.name: Double displacement vs single displacement
concepts.simple_answer: Ch 3 displacement is single — one element replaces another. Ch 1 double displacement swaps ions.

visual.formula: Single: Zn + CuSO₄ | Double: AB + CD → AD + CB

concepts.example: Zn + CuSO₄ is single displacement.
concepts.remember: One metal replaces another metal ion.
concepts.common_confusion: Precipitation reactions are double displacement.

concepts.name: Exam — displacement reactions
concepts.simple_answer: Define displacement → Zn + CuSO₄ equation and observations → explain why Cu + ZnSO₄ no reaction → Activity 3.7.
concepts.example: Blue fades, red-brown Cu, Zn dissolves.
concepts.common_confusion: Always state which metal is more reactive.

concepts.name: Reactivity series definition
concepts.simple_answer: Reactivity series arranges metals in order of decreasing reactivity — most reactive at top.

visual.formula: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Hg > Ag

concepts.example: K and Na most reactive; Ag least reactive common metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Hydrogen included as reference point.

concepts.name: Full NCERT reactivity series
concepts.simple_answer: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag — memorise this order.

visual.formula: K Na Ca Mg Al Zn Fe Pb Cu Hg Ag
visual.note: Mnemonic: Please send charlie's monkeys and zebras...

concepts.example: Mnemonic helps recall order.
concepts.remember: Hydrogen position between Pb and Cu.
concepts.common_confusion: Au and Pt even less reactive than Ag.

concepts.name: Most reactive metals — K, Na, Ca
concepts.simple_answer: Potassium, sodium, and calcium react vigorously with cold water and air.
concepts.example: Na stored under kerosene.
concepts.remember: Top three react with cold water.
concepts.common_confusion: Never handle Na/K without proper supervision.

concepts.name: Middle reactivity — Mg, Al, Zn, Fe
concepts.simple_answer: Magnesium, aluminium, zinc, and iron react with acids; Al needs oxide removed; Fe rusts.

visual.label: Mg, Al, Zn, Fe — middle reactivity

concepts.example: Zn and Fe common in displacement examples.
concepts.remember: React with dilute acids — above hydrogen.
concepts.common_confusion: Al protected by Al₂O₃ layer.

concepts.name: Least reactive — Cu, Hg, Ag
concepts.simple_answer: Copper, mercury, and silver do not react with dilute acids or cold water; found free in nature.
concepts.example: Silver and gold jewellery — unreacted metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Cu reacts slowly with moist air — green patina.

concepts.name: Hydrogen in reactivity series
concepts.simple_answer: Hydrogen placed between lead and copper — metals above H displace H from dilute acids.

visual.formula: Metal above H → reacts with dilute acid → H₂

concepts.example: Zn above H — gives H₂ with HCl.
concepts.remember: Below H — no H₂ from dilute acid.
concepts.common_confusion: H not a metal but used as benchmark.

concepts.name: Reactivity series predicts reactions
concepts.simple_answer: Series predicts: water reactions, acid reactions, displacement, and extraction method.
concepts.example: K reacts with cold water; Cu does not.
concepts.common_confusion: Higher metal reduces lower metal oxide.

concepts.name: Relative reactivity comparisons
concepts.simple_answer: Exam asks: 'Which is more reactive, Zn or Fe?' — Zn is higher in series.
concepts.example: Zn displaces Fe? No — both react with acid but Zn displaces Cu.
concepts.common_confusion: Compare positions, not properties alone.

concepts.name: Reactivity and extraction link
concepts.simple_answer: Highly reactive metals (Na, Ca, Al) extracted by electrolysis; less reactive by reduction with C.
concepts.example: Al from bauxite by electrolysis.
concepts.remember: More reactive = harder to extract = electrolysis.
concepts.common_confusion: Cu and Hg extracted by heating sulphide ore.

concepts.name: Exam — reactivity series
concepts.simple_answer: Write full series → explain one reaction prediction (water/acid/displacement) → compare two metals → mnemonic.
concepts.example: K Na Ca Mg Al Zn Fe Pb Cu Hg Ag — write completely.
concepts.common_confusion: Include H position between Pb and Cu.

days.title: How Metals and Non-metals React — Ions

concepts.name: How metals and non-metals react
concepts.simple_answer: Metals and non-metals react by transfer of electrons — metal loses electrons, non-metal gains.

visual.formula: Metal → loses e⁻ | Non-metal → gains e⁻

concepts.example: Na gives electron to Cl forming NaCl.
concepts.common_confusion: Not sharing — transfer (ionic compounds).

concepts.name: Metal atoms lose electrons
concepts.simple_answer: Metal atoms have 1–3 valence electrons — easily lost to form positive ions (cations).
concepts.example: Sodium loses 1 electron → Na⁺.
concepts.common_confusion: More reactive metals lose electrons more easily.

concepts.name: Non-metal atoms gain electrons
concepts.simple_answer: Non-metal atoms have 5–7 valence electrons — gain electrons to complete octet, form negative ions (anions).
concepts.example: Chlorine gains 1 electron → Cl⁻.
concepts.common_confusion: Gaining electrons completes outer shell.

concepts.name: Formation of sodium chloride NaCl
concepts.simple_answer: Sodium donates 1 e⁻ to chlorine — Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract electrostatically forming NaCl.
concepts.example: Table salt — ionic crystal lattice.
concepts.remember: Na⁺ + Cl⁻ held by electrostatic force.
concepts.common_confusion: NaCl solid — ions packed in crystal.

concepts.name: Formation of magnesium chloride MgCl₂
concepts.simple_answer: Magnesium loses 2 electrons; two chlorine atoms each gain 1 — Mg²⁺ and 2Cl⁻ form MgCl₂.
concepts.example: MgCl₂ used in tofu and road de-icing.
concepts.remember: Balance electrons: Mg gives 2, each Cl takes 1.
concepts.common_confusion: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ for neutral compound.

concepts.name: Electron dot structure — NaCl
concepts.simple_answer: Show Na with 1 dot (valence e⁻) transferring to Cl (7 dots → 8) — Na⁺ and Cl⁻ formed.
concepts.example: Draw Na atom, Cl atom, then ions.
concepts.common_confusion: Cl⁻ has 8 outer electrons after gaining.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds definition
concepts.simple_answer: Compounds formed by transfer of electrons between metal and non-metal — contain ions.
concepts.example: NaCl, MgO, CaCl₂ are ionic.
concepts.common_confusion: Not all metal-non-metal compounds ionic — SnCl₄ covalent (advanced).

concepts.name: Electrovalency
concepts.simple_answer: Electrovalency is the number of electrons lost or gained — equals charge on ion.
concepts.example: Cl⁻ has electrovalency 1.
concepts.common_confusion: Same as valency for main group elements.

concepts.name: Compare metal vs non-metal electron behaviour
concepts.simple_answer: Metals: lose e⁻, form cations, low ionisation energy. Non-metals: gain e⁻, form anions, high electron affinity.
concepts.example: Na loses; Cl gains — opposite tendencies.
concepts.common_confusion: Metalloids can do both — borderline.

concepts.name: Exam — electron transfer and ions
concepts.simple_answer: Explain electron transfer → NaCl formation with equations → dot structure → define ionic compound.
concepts.example: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻; Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl.
concepts.common_confusion: State cation and anion clearly.

concepts.name: Physical state of ionic compounds
concepts.simple_answer: Ionic compounds are generally solid at room temperature — hard crystalline solids.
concepts.example: NaCl, MgO, CaCl₂ are white crystalline solids.
concepts.common_confusion: Crystal lattice of alternating ions.

concepts.name: High melting and boiling points
concepts.simple_answer: Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points — strong electrostatic forces between ions.
concepts.example: NaCl melts at 801°C — very high.
concepts.remember: Strong ionic bonds need much heat to break.
concepts.common_confusion: High mp distinguishes ionic from covalent.

concepts.name: Solubility in water
concepts.simple_answer: Most ionic compounds dissolve in water — water molecules surround ions (hydration).
concepts.example: NaCl dissolves readily in water.
concepts.common_confusion: Some insoluble: AgCl, BaSO₄ — exceptions.

concepts.name: Electrical conductivity — solid vs molten
concepts.simple_answer: Ionic compounds do NOT conduct electricity in solid state; DO conduct when molten or dissolved in water.

visual.note: Ions must be free to move

concepts.example: NaCl solid — bulb off; NaCl solution — bulb glows.
concepts.remember: Ions fixed in solid; mobile when molten/dissolved.
concepts.common_confusion: Most common exam trap in Ch 3.

concepts.name: Why solid ionic compounds do not conduct
concepts.simple_answer: In solid ionic crystal, ions are fixed in lattice positions — cannot move to carry charge.
concepts.example: NaCl crystal — Na⁺ and Cl⁻ locked in place.
concepts.common_confusion: Metallic solids conduct — different mechanism.

concepts.name: Why molten ionic compounds conduct
concepts.simple_answer: When melted, ionic lattice breaks — ions free to move toward electrodes carrying charge.
concepts.example: Electrolysis of molten NaCl gives Na and Cl₂.
concepts.common_confusion: Basis for electrolytic extraction.

concepts.name: Why aqueous ionic solutions conduct
concepts.simple_answer: Water dissolves ionic compound — ions surrounded by water molecules and free to move.
concepts.example: Salt water conducts — ions in solution.
concepts.common_confusion: Pure water alone conducts poorly.

concepts.name: Brittleness of ionic crystals
concepts.simple_answer: Ionic crystals are brittle — shatter when struck because ion layers shift and repel.
concepts.example: NaCl crystal shatters if hammered.
concepts.remember: Same charge ions align and repel — crack.
concepts.common_confusion: Contrast with malleable metals.

concepts.name: Properties summary table
concepts.simple_answer: Solid, high mp, soluble, conduct when molten/dissolved, brittle — five key ionic properties.

visual.formula: Solid | High mp | Soluble | Conduct (molten/aq) | Brittle

concepts.example: Memorise all five for long answer.
concepts.common_confusion: Graphite conducts in solid — not ionic.

concepts.name: Exam — properties of ionic compounds
concepts.simple_answer: List five properties → explain conductivity solid vs molten vs aqueous → NaCl example for each.
concepts.example: Solid NaCl insulator; NaCl(aq) conductor.
concepts.common_confusion: Conductivity trap — solid does NOT conduct.

days.title: Occurrence of Metals — Ores and Enrichment

concepts.name: Occurrence of metals in nature
concepts.simple_answer: Most metals found as compounds in earth's crust; only less reactive metals found free.
concepts.example: Al and Fe abundant as oxides; Au, Ag rare as free metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Abundance: Al > Fe > Ca in crust.

concepts.name: Minerals and ores
concepts.simple_answer: Mineral is natural compound of metal; ore is mineral from which metal extracted profitably.

visual.formula: Mineral → may be ore if economical
visual.note: All ores are minerals; not all minerals are ores

concepts.example: Bauxite is ore of aluminium.
concepts.common_confusion: Haematite is ore; other iron minerals may not be.

concepts.name: Gangue definition
concepts.simple_answer: Gangue is unwanted earthy material (sand, rocky impurities) mixed with ore.
concepts.example: Sand and clay in iron ore.
concepts.common_confusion: Also called matrix or impurities.

concepts.name: Enrichment of ores
concepts.simple_answer: Ores concentrated by removing gangue — methods: hydraulic washing, magnetic separation, froth flotation.
concepts.example: Magnetic separation for magnetic ores like magnetite.
concepts.common_confusion: Froth flotation for sulphide ores.

concepts.name: Important ores — aluminium
concepts.simple_answer: Bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O) is main ore of aluminium — most abundant metal in crust.
concepts.example: Aluminium from bauxite by electrolysis.
concepts.common_confusion: Al most abundant metal — from bauxite.

concepts.name: Important ores — iron
concepts.simple_answer: Haematite (Fe₂O₃) and magnetite (Fe₃O₄) are main ores of iron.
concepts.example: Blast furnace uses haematite.
concepts.common_confusion: Magnetite magnetic — separated magnetically.

concepts.name: Important ores — copper and zinc
concepts.simple_answer: Copper from copper pyrites (CuFeS₂); zinc from zinc blende (ZnS).

visual.formula: Copper pyrites: CuFeS₂ | Zinc blende: ZnS

concepts.example: Sulphide ores roasted before reduction.
concepts.remember: Cu and Zn from sulphide ores.
concepts.common_confusion: Roasting converts sulphide to oxide.

concepts.name: Calcination definition
concepts.simple_answer: Calcination heats ore in absence or limited air — carbonate/hydroxide ore decomposes to oxide.
concepts.example: Carbonate ores calcined before reduction.
concepts.common_confusion: Opposite of roasting — no air.

concepts.name: Roasting definition
concepts.simple_answer: Roasting heats sulphide ore in presence of air — sulphide converts to oxide.
concepts.example: Sulphide ores roasted to oxide.
concepts.common_confusion: Roasting for sulphides; calcination for carbonates.

concepts.name: Exam — ores and enrichment
concepts.simple_answer: Define ore and gangue → name three ores with formulae → enrichment methods → calcination vs roasting.
concepts.example: Bauxite, haematite, zinc blende examples.
concepts.common_confusion: Gangue removal before extraction.

concepts.name: Extracting metals — overview
concepts.simple_answer: Method of extraction depends on reactivity — highly reactive need electrolysis; moderate use C/CO reduction.
concepts.example: K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al — electrolysis.
concepts.common_confusion: Less reactive = reduction with carbon.

concepts.name: Reduction of metal oxides
concepts.simple_answer: Metal oxide reduced to free metal by heating with carbon, carbon monoxide, or more reactive metal.

visual.formula: Metal oxide + Reducing agent → Metal + Oxide of reducer
visual.note: Reduction = loss of oxygen from metal compound

concepts.example: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ in blast furnace.
concepts.common_confusion: C and CO common reducing agents.

concepts.name: Iron extraction — blast furnace
concepts.simple_answer: Haematite reduced by CO in blast furnace at high temperature — molten iron collected.
concepts.example: Coke produces CO which reduces iron ore.
concepts.common_confusion: Limestone removes silica as slag.

concepts.name: Zinc extraction — reduction
concepts.simple_answer: Zinc oxide from roasted zinc blende reduced by heating with carbon.
concepts.example: Zn distils off and collected.
concepts.remember: ZnO reduced by C at high temperature.
concepts.common_confusion: Zn boils below reduction temperature — distillation.

concepts.name: Copper extraction — sulphide route
concepts.simple_answer: Copper sulphide ore roasted to oxide, then reduced; low reactivity allows heating alone.
concepts.example: Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂ (self-reduction).
concepts.remember: Cu extracted by heating sulphide ore.
concepts.common_confusion: Some Cu found native — low reactivity.

concepts.name: Mercury extraction
concepts.simple_answer: Cinnabar (HgS) roasted to HgO, then HgO decomposes to Hg on heating.
concepts.example: Mercury liquid at room temperature.
concepts.remember: HgO unstable on heating — releases Hg.
concepts.common_confusion: Hg toxic — historical thermometers.

concepts.name: Electrolysis for highly reactive metals
concepts.simple_answer: Na, Ca, Mg, and Al extracted by electrolysis of molten chloride or oxide — too reactive for C reduction.
concepts.example: Al from bauxite via electrolysis in cryolite.
concepts.remember: Electrolysis for K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al.
concepts.common_confusion: Large electricity consumption — expensive.

concepts.name: Sodium extraction — electrolysis
concepts.simple_answer: Molten NaCl electrolysed — sodium at cathode, chlorine at anode.
concepts.example: Same brine electrolysis as chlor-alkali (Ch 2).
concepts.remember: Molten NaCl — not aqueous for Na metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Na collects at cathode — very reactive.

concepts.name: Activity series and reducing agent strength
concepts.simple_answer: More reactive metal can reduce less reactive metal oxide — thermite: Al reduces Fe₂O₃.
concepts.example: Thermite weld railway tracks.
concepts.remember: Al more reactive than Fe — reduces Fe₂O₃.
concepts.common_confusion: Very exothermic — molten iron produced.

concepts.name: Exam — extracting metals
concepts.simple_answer: Link reactivity to method → blast furnace equation → electrolysis for Al/Na → calcination/roasting before reduction.
concepts.example: Fe: blast furnace; Al: electrolysis.
concepts.remember: Three methods: electrolysis, C reduction, heating.
concepts.common_confusion: Always name ore and write key equation.

concepts.name: Electrolytic refining definition
concepts.simple_answer: Electrolytic refining purifies impure metal using electrolysis — pure metal deposited at cathode.

visual.formula: Impure metal anode → Pure metal cathode

concepts.example: Pure Cu deposited from CuSO₄ solution.
concepts.remember: Anode dissolves; cathode gains pure metal.
concepts.common_confusion: Used for Cu, Zn, Ag, Au refining.

concepts.name: Electrolytic refining of copper
concepts.simple_answer: Impure Cu anode, pure Cu cathode, CuSO₄ electrolyte — pure Cu plates on cathode.

visual.formula: Anode: impure Cu → Cathode: pure Cu

concepts.example: Insoluble impurities fall as anode mud.
concepts.common_confusion: Anode mud contains Ag and Au — valuable.

concepts.name: Anode mud
concepts.simple_answer: Insoluble impurities (gold, silver) settle below anode during electrolytic refining — called anode mud.
concepts.example: Gold and silver recovered from anode mud.
concepts.remember: Less reactive impurities do not dissolve.
concepts.common_confusion: Anode mud economically valuable.

concepts.name: Corrosion definition
concepts.simple_answer: Corrosion is gradual destruction of metals by chemical reaction with environment — moisture and air.
concepts.example: Iron rusts; silver tarnishes; copper patina.
concepts.common_confusion: Corrosion is electrochemical process.

concepts.name: Rusting of iron
concepts.simple_answer: Rusting is corrosion of iron — forms hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust) in presence of oxygen and water.
concepts.example: Brown flaky rust on iron gates and nails.
concepts.remember: Needs both O₂ and H₂O for rust.
concepts.common_confusion: Rust is porous — corrosion continues underneath.

concepts.name: Conditions for rusting
concepts.simple_answer: Iron rusts when both oxygen and water present — dry air or pure water alone insufficient.
concepts.example: Nail in dry air — no rust; in boiled water + oil — no rust.
concepts.common_confusion: Salt water accelerates rusting.

concepts.name: Other metal corrosion
concepts.simple_answer: Silver tarnishes (Ag₂S from H₂S); copper green patina (basic copper carbonate); aluminium protected by Al₂O₃.
concepts.example: Silver blackens with sulphur compounds.
concepts.common_confusion: Green on copper = CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂ patina.

concepts.name: Economic cost of corrosion
concepts.simple_answer: Corrosion damages bridges, cars, pipelines — billions spent on replacement and repair worldwide.
concepts.example: Rusted bridge structures need replacement.
concepts.common_confusion: Galvanisation and painting save money.

concepts.name: Compare refining and corrosion
concepts.simple_answer: Refining purifies metal intentionally; corrosion destroys metal unintentionally — both involve electrochemistry.
concepts.example: Electrolysis controls deposition in refining.
concepts.common_confusion: Both involve ion movement and redox.

concepts.name: Exam — refining and corrosion
concepts.simple_answer: Explain electrolytic refining of Cu → rusting equation and conditions → economic impact of corrosion.
concepts.example: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2xH₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O must-know.
concepts.common_confusion: State both O₂ and H₂O needed for rust.

days.title: Prevention of Corrosion and Exam Review

concepts.name: Galvanisation
concepts.simple_answer: Galvanisation coats iron with thin layer of zinc — Zn corrodes instead of Fe (sacrificial protection).
concepts.example: Galvanised buckets and roof sheets.
concepts.common_confusion: Scratch exposes Fe — Zn still protects nearby.

concepts.name: Painting and oiling
concepts.simple_answer: Paint, grease, or oil layer blocks air and moisture from reaching metal surface.
concepts.example: Painted iron gates resist rust longer.
concepts.remember: Physical barrier prevents O₂ and H₂O contact.
concepts.common_confusion: Must renew paint when chipped.

concepts.name: Alloying to prevent corrosion
concepts.simple_answer: Alloying makes metal resistant to corrosion — stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni) resists rust.
concepts.example: Stainless steel utensils do not rust.
concepts.common_confusion: Alloying changes properties — also increases hardness.

concepts.name: Chromium plating
concepts.simple_answer: Thin chromium layer on iron/nickel — shiny, hard, corrosion-resistant surface.
concepts.example: Chrome-plated bathroom fittings.
concepts.remember: Cr layer prevents rust and looks polished.
concepts.common_confusion: Different from galvanisation — Cr not sacrificial.

concepts.name: Sacrificial protection
concepts.simple_answer: More reactive metal (Zn, Mg) connected to iron — corrodes preferentially protecting iron.
concepts.example: Magnesium blocks on ship hulls.
concepts.common_confusion: Used on pipelines and ships.

concepts.name: Storing reactive metals
concepts.simple_answer: Na and K stored under kerosene; phosphorus under water — prevents reaction with air.
concepts.example: Na cuts stored in kerosene bottle.
concepts.common_confusion: Same principle as painting — block environment.

concepts.name: Unit 3 exam — physical properties summary
concepts.simple_answer: Metals: lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, good conductors. Non-metals: opposite + graphite/iodine exceptions.
concepts.example: Activity 3.1–3.4 cover all physical tests.
concepts.common_confusion: Graphite conducts; iodine lustrous.

concepts.name: Unit 3 exam — reactions summary
concepts.simple_answer: Air: metal + O₂ → oxide. Water: Na/K/Ca cold; Fe steam. Acid: salt + H₂. Displacement: more reactive wins.
concepts.example: Zn + CuSO₄ displacement classic.
concepts.common_confusion: Cu no reaction with dilute acid or ZnSO₄.

concepts.name: Unit 3 exam — ions and extraction summary
concepts.simple_answer: Electron transfer → ionic compounds. Properties: solid, high mp, conduct molten/aq. Extraction by reactivity.
concepts.example: Al electrolysis; Fe blast furnace.
concepts.common_confusion: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2xH₂O → rust equation.

concepts.name: Unit 3 complete
concepts.simple_answer: Unit 3 Metals and Non-metals complete — all 160 cards; proceed to Practice when unlocked.
concepts.example: 200 MCQs in bank when available.
concepts.common_confusion: Review reactivity series, ionic properties, and rust prevention.
